A pattern I keep noticing in the daily scan: it's not always a brand new AI startup hiring its first ML engineer.
Increasingly it's an established product that already works well, something like an adtech platform or a healthtech company, adding a new LLM or agentic layer on top of it. And the senior hire they need isn't just an ML engineer, or just a domain expert. It's both in one person: deep knowledge of the existing product (fraud detection, clinical data, whatever the domain is) plus hands on production LLM experience.
That exact combination barely shows up on a job board. It's a small, passive pool, and most internal hiring processes are built to search for one skill set, not the overlap of two.
For specialist recruiters, that overlap is the mandate. Whoever already has two or three people like this warm in their pipeline has real leverage most recruiters don't.

The platform served multiple enterprise clients, but every client expected complete data isolation.

Inference performance met every SLA.

The challenge wasn't performance.
It was isolation.

Every customer had different business rules, documents, permissions, and compliance requirements. The platform had to ensure that retrieval, inference, logging, and cached data remained strictly separated across tenants without affecting scalability or operational efficiency.

I worked on strengthening the platform by implementing tenant-aware authentication, metadata-based access controls, isolated retrieval pipelines, scoped vector indexes, secure inference boundaries, and comprehensive auditing to ensure every request accessed only the data it was authorized to use.

The objective wasn't simply:
"Can the platform support multiple customers?"

The better question was:
"Can every customer trust that their AI environment is completely isolated from every other customer?"

That experience reinforced an important lesson:
Enterprise AI isn't only measured by intelligence. It's measured by security, governance, and trust.

Building production AI for regulated industries requires architecture that scales without compromising privacy, compliance, or customer confidence.

The AI Conundrum | Post 5 

There are only 2 options, you hire a driver/chauffer, or you learn to drive.
When it comes to AI, the CXO’s often face this challenge "We can't find the AI talent."

Any new technology goes through this phase, where the talent pool becomes the resource and technology becomes the commodity. AI is currently a scarce resource yet a commodity, by the AI skills are definitely a scarce resource.

You would have heard the absurd salaries being offered by the Big Tech, while I agree with the demand for AI engineers, ML researchers, and data scientists has never been higher and the salaries are rising crazily.

However, I think most enterprises are solving the wrong problem. The strategy of hiring your way out of it is flawed, while the AI talent war is real. You do not need an army of AI engineers. You need a handful of the right ones — and a workforce that knows how to work alongside them.

The enterprises that are actually scaling AI are not the ones with the biggest AI teams. They are the ones that figured out, What to hire for — and what to build internally.  Like its good to learn to drive, but its also okay to hire an experienced driver, if you are driving through the mountainous roads.

You hire for the capabilities you cannot develop fast enough: ML infrastructure, model evaluation, AI safety, advanced fine-tuning. Everything else like prompt engineering, AI-augmented workflows, agent configuration, basic RAG pipelines — can be built through structured enablement of your existing teams.

AI literacy is the new digital literacy and it is not optional.

1.      The product manager who understands how to work with an AI agent is ten times more effective than the one who doesn't. 
2.      The sales leader who knows how to interrogate an AI-generated forecast is dramatically more valuable than the one who takes it at face value.

Enterprise cannot transform by simply hiring AI talent, they can transform by democratizing AI across functions. 

Enterprises need to think away from hiring and drive towards re-skilling and upskilling and redesigning the functions and departments and the processes that kept them going so far, may not last long.

I'd love to hear what's actually working and how are you solving this within your organization.

author: Vikram Pandey
text:
Token Economics of #Resume Parsing: A Satire
रेज़्यूमे तो AI ने लिखा, पर इंटरव्यू में टोकन ख़त्म हो गए। 😆 

Had seen your Job Description… My AI engine ensured every keyword was patched in correctly -“Agile,” “Blockchain,” “Leadership,” “Agentic,” “Builder” sprinkled like masala on a street‑side chaat.
Then you receive the resume. You “spend tokens” to parse it… only to discover the exact same keywords, deliberately fed in for you to see.
Simple Use Case of Token Misutilisation 😉
The Comedy of Resume Parsing
Recruiter:  “Wow, this candidate knows Agile, Scrum, Kanban, DevOps, Cloud, AI, ML, NLP, IoT, AR/VR, and maybe even UFO engineering.” Reality: Candidate just ran a keyword patch script. AI Parser: “Thank you for your 1,500 tokens. Here’s a JSON file confirming the candidate knows… Agile, Scrum, Kanban…” Outcome: Zero new insight. Maximum token burn.
Classic Misuses – Don’t Tell Me You Realised It Now.

Buzzword Bingo: Resume reads like a startup pitch deck — “Disruption, Innovation, Unicorn, Synergy.”
Copy‑Paste Certifications: Same AWS certificate pasted thrice in different fonts.
Job Title Inflation: “Global Technology Evangelist” = Intern who once reset a router.
Skill Overload: Candidate lists 47 programming languages but can’t debug a print statement.
#Leadership/#Management
If your hiring funnel is just keyword‑matching, you’re not building teams you’re building token sinks.
 Winning organisations aren’t those that parse resumes faster; they’re those that filter noise smarter.
The real differentiator is not how many resumes you parse, but how many leaders you groom.

Closing Thought
We built AI to parse resumes. Candidates built AI to stuff resumes. Recruiters now spend tokens to confirm what they already suspected: the resume was engineered for the parser, not for the job.
💡 For CHROs and CXOs: The organisations that win are not those that “burn tokens” on parsing, but those that re‑engineer hiring to spot substance over syntax. Because fixing the hiring process is the first step to fixing the leadership pipeline , and that’s how winning teams are built.
